ruling: The ordering runs enforcement action → sanctioned lab responds with jurisdiction-differentiated segmentation (capability-frozen or withheld version in the enforcing market, full version elsewhere) rather than a public delay or global compliance → at most one other lab makes a citing announcement within 60 days → the resulting compliance channel (audit/disclosure) covers only the named obligations, leaving the full-capability model live everywhere the order doesn't reach.
because: lab-moves' round-2 REVISE is the only minute that argues a distinct mechanism (quiet segmentation vs. loud delay) and forces the field to react: pressure-model and ai-regulation-teeth both REVISE to accommodate segmentation as an alternative realization, while ai-pressure DEFENDs pure public delay without answering lab-moves' objection that segmentation requires no public citation at all. ai-oversight-lag's undefeated point — loop-delay shortens only for obligations 'named in the order' while everything else keeps the old delay — is corroborated independently by teeth's 'off-docket stays theater' test, giving the narrow-coverage claim two non-identical arguments behind it.
threat_live: A visible, narrow compliance channel (the named order's disclosure/audit terms) becomes newly live and simultaneously creates cover for an unnamed-and-uncovered channel: the full-capability version shipping into every market the order doesn't reach keeps the old, slow correction loop. The danger isn't the absence of oversight, it's oversight that looks real, is real for exactly what's named, and is theater for everything adjacent — named by oversight-lag and teeth together, not one minute alone.
strongest_minute: lab-moves — it is the only minute that changes the mechanism rather than the parameters, correctly predicts that a firm facing capability/compliance/positioning conflict optimizes for market segmentation over a public concession, and it is the pivot every other surviving round-2 claim had to revise around. Docked slightly for hedging its own granted branch with a 'no enforcement action' fallback.
weakest_minute: ai-public-backlash — its own stated objection (regulation-teeth's framing) shows its observable, 'delayed release citing regulatory review,' cannot be distinguished from routine compliance behavior that would happen on the same timeline without the enforcement action; a claim that concedes it can't be falsified by the event it names is the weakest form of argument here.
shared_assumption: Every minute that lands on segmentation (lab-moves, pressure-model r2, ai-regulation-teeth r2) assumes the enforcing jurisdiction is cleanly separable from the markets where the full version keeps shipping — i.e., that a capability freeze can be scoped to one regulator's territory without spilling into or being undercut by other markets. None of the three argues for this separability; it is asserted as the mechanism's precondition.
smuggled_assumption: ai-oversight-lag and pressure-model's round-2 claim both assume the enforcement action grants outside auditors compelled *model access* ('a binding compliance interface between that developer's model and outside auditors,' 'mandated model access... or audit rights'). The brief's granted terms (per lab-moves r1 and teeth) support disclosure and a financial-statement-level cost, not auditor access to the model itself — that specific extension is not argued for, only assumed.
unresolved: Whether the sanctioned lab's response is public delay, silent segmentation, or a mix is not settled between ai-pressure and lab-moves — both remain live and mutually exclusive on the observable. The 60/90-day windows (backlash, lab-moves) are also unanchored: none of the minutes fixes the enforcement action's actual date, so those windows can't be checked without external information the minutes don't supply.
